subject: C++ Programming & Object-Oriented Programming
exam_relevance: 10-12 questions expected in BPSC TRE CS exam

questions.question: Which OOP concept binds data and functions that manipulate data together into a single unit called a class?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Encapsulation wraps data and methods into a single unit (class). It is a fundamental OOP principle in Balaguruswamy C++.

questions.question: Which OOP concept allows a class to acquire properties and behaviours of another class?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Inheritance enables a derived class to acquire properties of a base class, promoting code reuse. (Balaguruswamy Ch.6)

questions.question: Which OOP concept means 'showing only essential features and hiding implementation details'?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Abstraction hides complexity by exposing only essential features. Example: using a car without knowing the engine internals.

questions.question: Which OOP concept means 'one name, many forms'?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Polymorphism means 'one name, many forms'. It allows functions or operators to behave differently based on context.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key benefit of encapsulation in OOP?

options.B: Data hiding and protection from accidental modification
options.C: Ability to define multiple functions with the same name
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Encapsulation's primary benefit is data hiding — private members are inaccessible from outside the class, protecting data integrity.

questions.question: In C++, compile-time polymorphism is achieved through which of the following?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Both function overloading (B) and operator overloading (C) achieve compile-time (static) polymorphism. Virtual functions give runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Object-Oriented Programming?

options.A: Data and functions are treated as separate entities
options.B: Programs are organised around objects rather than functions
options.C: It follows top-down approach like structured programming
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: OOP organises programs around objects. Structured programming uses top-down/function-centric approach. OOP is bottom-up.

questions.question: Which OOP feature helps in achieving runtime polymorphism in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime polymorphism via late binding. The function call is resolved at runtime based on the actual object type.

questions.question: In C++, a class is a _____ and an object is a _____ of that class.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A class is a user-defined blueprint/template. An object is an instance (variable) of a class. (Balaguruswamy, Ch. 5)

questions.question: Which of the following languages supports all four OOP pillars: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: C++ fully supports all four OOP pillars. C is procedural and does not natively support OOP. Assembly is low-level.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about OOP is CORRECT?

options.A: OOP emphasises on functions rather than data
options.B: In OOP, data moves freely from function to function
options.C: OOP follows a bottom-up approach in program design
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: OOP follows a bottom-up approach. It emphasises data over functions, and data is not freely accessible (encapsulation protects it).

questions.question: Which concept in OOP allows the same interface to be used for different underlying data types?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows the same interface (function/operator name) to work with different types, enabling flexible and reusable code.

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for members of a class in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In C++, the default access specifier for class members is private. For struct, it is public. (Balaguruswamy, Ch. 5)

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define a class in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The keyword 'class' is used to define a class in C++. 'struct' also creates a class-like type but with public default access.

questions.question: Members declared as 'private' in a class are accessible:

options.A: Within the class and all derived classes
options.C: Only within the class itself (member functions of that class)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Private members are accessible only within the same class. Derived classes cannot access them directly (use protected for that).

questions.question: Members declared as 'protected' in a class are accessible:

options.A: Within the class and its derived classes
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Protected members are accessible within the class and its derived classes, but not from outside the class hierarchy.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly defines a class named 'Student' in C++?

options.A: class Student( int roll; public: void show(); );
options.B: class Student { int roll; public: void show(); };
options.C: Class Student { int roll; public: void show(); };
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Class definition uses lowercase 'class' keyword with curly braces and semicolon at end. 'Class' (uppercase) is invalid in C++.

questions.question: A member function defined outside the class uses which operator to associate with the class?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The scope resolution operator (::) is used to define a member function outside the class: void ClassName::funcName() { }

questions.question: To access a member of an object using a pointer to that object, which operator is used?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Arrow operator (->) accesses members via pointer. Dot operator (.) accesses members via object directly. e.g., ptr->show();

questions.question: How many objects can be created from a single class in C++?

options.B: Any number (multiple objects can be created)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Multiple objects can be created from a single class. Each object has its own copy of data members but shares member functions.

questions.question: In C++, which of the following is true about static data members of a class?

options.A: They are shared by all objects of the class
options.B: They must be defined outside the class
options.C: Only one copy exists regardless of how many objects are created
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Static data members: shared by all objects (A), must be defined outside class (B), only one copy exists (C) — all three are correct.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about 'public' access specifier in a class?

options.A: Members are accessible only inside the class
options.B: Members are accessible only in derived classes
options.C: Members are accessible from anywhere in the program
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Public members are accessible from anywhere in the program — inside the class, in derived classes, and from main() or any function.

questions.question: In C++, the class that inherits properties of another class is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The class that inherits is called Derived class (also called child/sub class). The class being inherited from is Base/Parent/Super class.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct syntax for public inheritance in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: C++ uses colon (:) syntax for inheritance: class Derived : access_specifier Base { }. 'extends' is Java syntax, not C++.

questions.question: Which of the following are CORRECT syntax options for defining inheritance in C++? (From BPSC TRE 1.0)

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are valid C++ inheritance syntaxes. Without specifier it defaults to private. D is correct as A, B, and C are all valid.

questions.question: When a class inherits from only ONE base class, it is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Single inheritance: one derived class inherits from one base class. Multiple: inherits from more than one base class.

questions.question: When class C inherits from class B, and class B inherits from class A, it is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Multilevel: A→B→C (chain). Multiple: D inherits from both B and C. Hierarchical: multiple derived from same base.

questions.question: When more than one class inherits from the SAME base class, it is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Hierarchical: One base class → multiple derived classes (B, C both inherit from A). Multiple: one class inherits from multiple bases.

questions.question: In C++ public inheritance, public members of the base class become _____ in the derived class.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In public inheritance: public→public, protected→protected, private→inaccessible. Access level is preserved for public members.

questions.question: In C++ private inheritance, public members of the base class become _____ in the derived class.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In private inheritance, all accessible base class members (public and protected) become private in the derived class.

questions.question: The 'diamond problem' in C++ occurs due to which type of inheritance?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Diamond problem: class D inherits from B and C, both inherit from A — two copies of A's data in D. Solved by virtual base class.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to prevent duplication of base class data in multiple/hybrid inheritance (diamond problem)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Virtual base class (using 'virtual' keyword) ensures only one copy of base class is shared in diamond inheritance hierarchy.

questions.question: Which type of inheritance combines multiple types (e.g., multiple + multilevel) in a single hierarchy?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Hybrid inheritance is a combination of two or more types of inheritance (e.g., multiple + multilevel). It may cause diamond problem.

questions.question: Private members of a base class in public inheritance are _____ in the derived class.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Private members are inherited (occupy memory in derived object) but cannot be accessed directly. Access via public/protected base functions.

questions.question: Function overloading in C++ is an example of which type of polymorphism?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Function overloading is resolved at compile time (static/early binding), hence it is compile-time (static) polymorphism.

questions.question: Virtual functions in C++ are used to achieve:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime (dynamic) polymorphism via late binding — the correct function is selected at runtime based on object type.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to declare a virtual function in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The 'virtual' keyword before a base class member function makes it virtual, enabling runtime polymorphism through overriding.

questions.question: Operator overloading in C++ allows:

options.A: Giving additional meaning to existing operators for user-defined types
options.B: Defining new operators not present in C++
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Operator overloading redefines existing operators for user-defined types. New operators cannot be created; precedence cannot be changed.

questions.question: Which of the following operators CANNOT be overloaded in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Operators that cannot be overloaded: :: (scope resolution), . (dot), .* (pointer-to-member), ?: (ternary), sizeof. ++ and [] can be overloaded.

questions.question: Function overriding in C++ occurs when:

options.A: A derived class defines a function with the same name and signature as in the base class
options.B: Two functions in the same class have the same name but different parameters
options.C: A function is called using a pointer to base class
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Function overriding: derived class redefines base class function with identical name and signature. Overloading has different parameters.

questions.question: A pure virtual function in C++ is declared as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pure virtual function syntax: virtual returnType funcName() = 0; A class with at least one pure virtual function is an abstract class.

questions.question: A class that contains at least one pure virtual function is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A class with at least one pure virtual function is called an abstract class. Objects of abstract class cannot be created.

questions.question: Which of the following about function overloading is CORRECT?

options.A: Overloaded functions must differ in number or type of parameters
options.B: Overloaded functions must have same number and type of parameters
options.C: Return type alone can distinguish overloaded functions in C++
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Overloaded functions must differ in number or type (or order) of parameters. Return type alone is NOT sufficient to overload a function.

questions.question: Early binding (static binding) in C++ is associated with:

options.A: Function overloading and normal (non-virtual) function calls
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Early/static binding: function call resolved at compile time. Function overloading and regular function calls use early binding.

questions.question: In C++, which of the following correctly describes late binding?

options.A: Function address is determined at compile time
options.B: It is used only with function overloading
options.C: Function is selected based on the actual object type at runtime
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Late binding (dynamic binding): function address resolved at runtime based on actual object pointed to, used with virtual functions.

questions.question: Which of the following operators is typically overloaded to display object data using cout?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The << (insertion/left-shift) operator is overloaded for cout to display object data. >> is overloaded for cin input.

questions.question: A constructor in C++ is a special member function that:

options.A: Destroys the object when it goes out of scope
options.B: Is automatically called when an object is created
options.C: Must be explicitly called by the programmer
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Constructor is automatically invoked when an object is created to initialise it. It has the same name as the class and no return type.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about constructors in C++?

options.A: Constructor has the same name as the class
options.B: Constructor has no return type (not even void)
options.C: Constructor is called automatically when an object is created
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are true: constructors have same name as class (A), no return type (B), and are called automatically on object creation (C).

questions.question: A constructor that takes no arguments is called a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Default constructor takes no arguments. If not defined, C++ provides an implicit default constructor. Parameterized takes arguments.

questions.question: A copy constructor takes as its argument:

options.B: A reference to another object of the same class
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Copy constructor signature: ClassName(const ClassName &obj). It takes a const reference to another object of the same class.

questions.question: A destructor in C++ is a special function that:

options.A: Has the same name as the class preceded by tilde (~)
options.B: Is called automatically when an object goes out of scope
options.C: Frees resources acquired by the object
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are true about destructors: name is ~ClassName (A), called automatically at object end of life (B), frees resources (C).

questions.question: Can a constructor be overloaded in C++?

options.A: Yes, a class can have multiple constructors with different parameter lists
options.B: Yes, but only with the same parameters
options.C: No, only one constructor is allowed per class
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Constructors can be overloaded — a class can have default, parameterized, and copy constructors, all with different signatures.

questions.question: In a multilevel inheritance (A → B → C), when an object of C is created, the order of constructor calls is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Constructors are called from base to derived: A first, then B, then C. Destructors are called in reverse order: C, B, A.

questions.question: In C++, if a class has dynamically allocated memory, which constructor should be explicitly defined to avoid shallow copy?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Copy constructor must be explicitly defined for deep copy when class has pointer members (dynamic memory) to avoid shared pointer issues.

questions.question: How many destructors can a class have in C++?

options.C: Two — one for static and one for dynamic objects
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A class can have only ONE destructor. Destructors cannot be overloaded — they take no parameters and have no return type.

questions.question: When is the destructor of an object called?

options.C: When object goes out of scope or is deleted
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Destructor is called when object goes out of scope (local objects) or when delete is used (dynamic objects). Cleans up resources.

questions.question: A friend function in C++:

options.A: Is a member function of the class
options.B: Can access private and protected members of the class
options.C: Is declared using the 'friend' keyword inside the class
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Friend function: not a member (A is false), but can access private/protected (B true), declared with 'friend' keyword inside class (C true). B and C correct.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about a friend function?

options.A: It is not a member of the class
options.B: It can access private members of the class
options.C: It is declared with the 'friend' keyword
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three (A, B, C) are correct about friend functions. It is NOT a member but IS granted access to private/protected members.

questions.question: The 'this' pointer in C++ refers to:

options.A: The base class of the current object
options.C: The address of the current calling object
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 'this' pointer holds the address of the object that invoked the member function. It is an implicit parameter in every non-static member function.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about 'this' pointer is CORRECT?

options.A: It is available in all member functions including static member functions
options.B: It points to the object for which the member function is called
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: B and C are correct. 'this' is NOT available in static functions (A is false). Static functions have no 'this' pointer.

questions.question: A friend function is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Friend functions are not member functions, so called without dot/arrow notation. The object is passed as an argument: friendFunc(obj).

questions.question: Can a friend function be a member of another class in C++?

options.A: No, friend functions must always be global
options.B: Yes, but only for public member functions
options.C: Yes, a member function of one class can be a friend of another class
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A member function of class X can be declared as a friend of class Y. This allows X's function to access Y's private members.

questions.question: Which of the following about 'this' pointer is FALSE?

options.A: It can be used to return a reference to the calling object
options.B: It is implicitly passed to all non-static member functions
options.C: It is available in static member functions
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 'this' pointer is NOT available in static member functions because static functions are not associated with any particular object.

questions.question: Friend classes in C++ allow:

options.A: Only public functions of the friend class to access private members
options.B: The friend class to inherit from the granting class
options.C: All member functions of the friend class to access private members of the granting class
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: When class A declares class B as friend, ALL member functions of B can access private/protected members of A. Friendship is not inheritance.

questions.question: Which operator is used to declare a pointer in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: * is used to declare a pointer: int *p; The & operator gives the address of a variable. -> accesses members via pointer.

questions.question: If int x = 10; and int *p = &x; then what does *p give?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: *p dereferences the pointer — gives the value at the address stored in p. Since p = &x and x = 10, *p = 10.

questions.question: Which operator gives the address of a variable in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: & (address-of operator) gives the memory address of a variable. e.g., int x=5; int *p=&x; — p stores address of x.

questions.question: Which keyword is used for dynamic memory allocation in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 'new' is C++ operator for dynamic allocation. 'malloc' is C function. Example: int *p = new int; allocates int on heap.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to free dynamically allocated memory in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 'delete' frees memory allocated by 'new'. 'free' is the C counterpart for 'malloc'. Use delete[] for arrays: delete[] p;

questions.question: To dynamically allocate an array of 5 integers in C++, the correct statement is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: new int[5] allocates array of 5 ints. new int(5) allocates one int initialised to 5. Square brackets [ ] are used for arrays.

questions.question: If Student *p = new Student; is used to create a dynamic object, how is a member function show() called?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Arrow operator (->) is used to access members through a pointer: p->show(). Dot (.) is used for objects, not pointers.

questions.question: A NULL pointer in C++ is:

options.A: A pointer to a void type
options.B: A pointer pointing to address 0 (or nullptr in C++11)
options.C: A pointer that has not been declared
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: NULL pointer points to address 0. In C++11, nullptr is preferred. A void pointer (void*) is different from a NULL pointer.

questions.question: In C++, int *p = new int[10]; then to free the memory, you should use:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: For array allocated with new[], use delete[] to free. delete p would cause undefined behavior. free() is for malloc only.

questions.question: A void pointer (void *) in C++:

options.C: Can store address of any data type
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: void* is a generic pointer that can hold the address of any data type. It must be cast to the appropriate type before dereferencing.

questions.question: Which header file is required for file handling in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: <fstream> header provides ifstream (input), ofstream (output), and fstream (both) for C++ file handling. stdio.h is for C.

questions.question: Which class is used to write data to a file in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ofstream (output file stream) is specifically for writing. fstream supports both reading and writing. Both B and C can write.

questions.question: Which file open mode in C++ opens a file for appending (adds data at the end)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ios::app opens file for appending — writes at end of file. ios::out truncates existing file. ios::in opens for reading.

questions.question: Which class is used to READ data from a file in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ifstream (input file stream) is used to read from files. ofstream is for output/writing. fstream handles both.

questions.question: Which file open mode is used to open a file for binary operations in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ios::binary opens the file in binary mode (no text translations). Used for binary files. ios::text is not a valid mode flag.

questions.question: In C++, which member function is used to check if a file has been opened successfully?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: is_open() returns true if the file is open. good() checks for no errors. fail() returns true if an operation failed.

questions.question: In C++, 'cout' stands for:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: cout stands for 'character output'. It is an object of the ostream class used for output. (BPSC TRE 2.0 — answer B)

questions.question: Which shortcut key is used to compile and run a C++ program in Turbo C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Ctrl+F9 compiles and runs in Turbo C++. Alt+F5 shows the user (output) screen. (BPSC TRE 1.0 — answer C)

questions.question: Which shortcut key is used to view the user (output) screen in Turbo C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Alt+F5 displays the user output screen in Turbo C++. Ctrl+F9 compiles and runs. These are frequently asked in BPSC TRE.

questions.question: What is the correct extension for a C++ source file?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Both .cpp (B) and .cxx (C) are valid C++ extensions. .c is for C language. In Turbo C++, .cpp is most commonly used.

questions.question: Which header file must be included to use cout and cin in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: <iostream> provides cout and cin. <stdio.h> is for C's printf/scanf. <conio.h> provides getch(), clrscr() (Turbo C++).

questions.question: What does the 'sizeof' operator return in C++?

options.A: The size in bytes of a data type or variable
options.B: The number of elements in an array
options.C: The value stored in the variable
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: sizeof returns the size in bytes of a type or variable. sizeof(int) is typically 2 (Turbo) or 4 (modern). It is a compile-time operator.

questions.question: In Turbo C++, sizeof(int) returns:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In Turbo C++ (16-bit), sizeof(int) = 2 bytes. In modern 32/64-bit compilers, sizeof(int) = 4 bytes.

questions.question: The insertion operator (<<) is used with which object in C++?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: << is used with cout (B) for standard output AND with cerr (C) for error output. >> (extraction) is used with cin.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid C++ data type?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three — int (A), float (B), and double (C) — are valid built-in C++ data types. All are correct.

questions.question: The 'using namespace std;' directive in C++ is used to:

options.B: Avoid writing std:: before cout, cin, etc.
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: using namespace std; allows using cout, cin without std:: prefix. It doesn't include libraries or define namespaces.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: a=5, b=3. a+b = 8. cout prints 8. No quotes around a+b, so it evaluates the expression.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: First cout prints 'Hello' then endl (newline). Second cout prints 'World'. Output: Hello on line 1, World on line 2.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: x++ is post-increment: prints x (10) then increments. After increment x=11. So output: 10 11.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Ternary: a>b is 4>2 = true, so prints a = 4.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Loop: i=1 (print 1), i=2 (print 2), i=3 (print 3), i=4 (4>3, stop). Output: 1 2 3 (with trailing space).

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: sizeof(int) = 2 in Turbo C++ (B→C), 4 in modern compilers (B). Both B and C are possible depending on compiler. D is correct.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: x=2. x*x = 4. 4+x = 4+2 = 6. x=6. cout prints 6.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: % is modulus operator. 10 % 3 = 1 (10 = 3*3 + 1, remainder is 1). cout prints 1.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: show(5) is called. x=5. x*2 = 10. cout prints 10.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Object created: constructor prints 'A '. Object goes out of scope at end of main: destructor prints '~A'. Output: A ~A.
